client: Lately, I've been avoiding family gatherings because being around everyone just makes me feel my grandmother's absence even more. It’s like her not being there is this huge void that no one else notices, and it’s hard to face. I’m not sure if talking about it will really help—it feels like nothing can fill that space she left.
therapist: I hear how deeply you're feeling your grandmother's absence, especially in those family moments that used to include her. It makes sense that being around everyone would highlight that loss so intensely—would you be willing to share what those gatherings were like when she was still with you?

client: She was always the one who... I don't know, made everything feel warm? Like she'd remember everyone's favorite foods and have this way of pulling people together. Now it's just... different. I don't see the point in going when it feels so obviously wrong without her there.
therapist: You've described her presence so beautifully—it sounds like she created this warm, loving glue that held family moments together. When you say it feels "obviously wrong" without her, I wonder if part of the pain comes from expecting gatherings to feel the same way they did when she was there?

client: Yeah, I guess I do expect it to feel the same, and it never does. But it's not just that—it's also like no one else seems to feel her absence as much as I do. That makes me feel even more alone in it. I don’t know if changing my expectations would really help—it’s not just about how things feel, it’s about missing *her*.
therapist: It sounds like you're carrying this grief in two ways—missing her deeply, while also feeling isolated because others don't seem to share that same intensity of loss. Have you noticed if there are particular moments when you feel her absence most sharply, versus times when the memories feel more comforting?

client: It's worst during holidays when she'd always make her special dishes, or when someone says "we're all here" because... we're not. The memories only feel comforting when I'm alone, honestly—when I'm with family and no one mentions her, it's like they've forgotten. But bringing her up feels like I'm ruining the mood.
therapist: I can hear how painful it is to feel like her memory isn’t being honored in those moments that were so tied to her presence. It sounds like being alone allows you to hold onto her in a way that feels safe, while being with family brings up that sense of disconnect. What do you think might happen if you shared a memory or mention of her during those gatherings, even if it feels risky?

client: I'm scared it would make everyone uncomfortable—like I'm the one who can't "move on" properly. But then again... maybe others are holding back too? It's just hard to be the first one to bring her up when no one else does. What if they don't respond the way I hope?
therapist: That fear of being met with silence or discomfort is completely understandable—it takes courage to be the first to voice something so tender. I wonder if there might be a small way to test this, like sharing just one simple memory to see how the room responds?

client: Maybe I could mention how she always burned the dinner rolls—every single time. Everyone used to tease her about it. But what if I say that and then... nothing? It hurts to think about her being forgotten, but it might hurt worse to have the silence confirm it.
therapist: That burned rolls memory is so specific and full of love—it's a beautiful way to invite others into remembering her. The silence you fear would be painful, but might there also be relief in knowing you've honored her, regardless of how others respond?

client: I guess there could be some relief in knowing I tried, but it still feels so risky. What if I’m the only one who misses her that much? I don’t want to make everyone uncomfortable, but I also don’t want to pretend like she wasn’t this huge part of our lives. It’s just... complicated, and I’m not sure if I’m ready to take that step yet.
therapist: It sounds like you're holding two truths—wanting to honor her importance while also protecting yourself from potential disappointment. That hesitation makes complete sense. What would need to feel different for you to know when the right moment to share might be?

client: Maybe if I saw even one other family member mention her first—just some small sign that it's okay to talk about her. Right now it feels like everyone's pretending she never existed, and that makes my grief feel... wrong somehow. I don't know how to be the one to break that silence all alone.
therapist: I hear how much you’re longing for some acknowledgment—that small sign that it’s safe to talk about her and that others remember her too. It’s so hard to carry that grief when it feels like you’re the only one honoring her memory. Have you noticed any moments where someone might have hinted at missing her, even subtly?

client: Now that you mention it, my cousin did bring up her apple pie once—how no one’s been able to make it taste the same. But then the conversation just moved on like it was nothing. It felt like a tiny crack in the silence, but I didn’t know how to keep it open without forcing it. Maybe others do miss her too, but we’re all just... stuck in this awkwardness.
therapist: That "tiny crack" you noticed is so important—it sounds like your cousin might have been testing the waters too, unsure how the family would respond. Grief can make us all hesitate like that, can't it? What do you imagine might happen if you and your cousin gently kept opening those cracks together?

client: I hadn’t thought about it that way—maybe my cousin was feeling the same hesitation I am. It’s just... what if we try to open those cracks and it still feels forced? I don’t want to make everyone uncomfortable or feel like I’m dragging the mood down. It’s hard to know how much to push when grief feels so personal.
therapist: It sounds like you're holding this careful balance between wanting connection and fearing disruption—which shows how deeply you care about both honoring your grandmother and respecting the family's mood. That middle ground between silence and forcing things is tricky to find—what if you started by sharing those memories with just your cousin first, where it might feel safer?
